chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
title: Will Vodery's score writing, Gershwin as copyist and his Penn degree
summary: Whaley and Hinton confirm Vodery wrote scores without mistakes, offered $10 per error, passed a bandmaster exam in twenty minutes, and lived on 141st Street.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, did you know anything about -- you know, I used to talk to Will Vodery, the great arranger?
Oh yes.
He told me that George Gershwin used to be his copyist, used to copy for him.
I guess he was. I met Bill, you know, it was in the army, and he's the first guy that I saw

stand up before a whole bunch of people and give me some manuscripts - and write just like a letter, and write. Don't make a mistake, and he said ten dollars for every mistake, and I said that's the greatest thing I have ever heard.
I've told many people in this town, but I'm so happy to hear you say this, it's a matter of record to verify that, because I worked with him at the Cotton Club.
Yeah, that's right.
Downtown.
And he said the same thing, he said if it was a mistake, the copyist made it, because he said that score was correct.
That's right -- and remember, I was down there, too, with him?
That's right, sure, Tom.
Yeah, Bill Vodery, to me one of the greatest.
Great arranger. Great orchestrator.
Yeah, Carl Towne said he was the greatest musician in the world.
Who was that? Earl who?
Earl Towne out of Vanity.
He wrote for Ziegfield -- for 23 years, he did all the Ziegfield shows, didn't he?
Yeah. Oh yeah. He graduated from
the University of Pennsylvania.
Is that so?

We were in the army, see, and all the bandleaders had to take an examination at Shaumont, see, and he did a two hour concert, examination -- he did in 20 minutes. The man said, 'where you going? You ain't finished' and he said, "Yeah, I finished it." Twenty minutes -- Bill Vodery.

I'm so glad to hear you say this, because we don't even have pictures, and especially for our young black people, that they should have some history of some fairly famous black people that came before them, as we don't have anything to tell them about him, so thank you for verifying what I said about him. What a tremendous musician he was.
Oh, everybody -- Bill Vodery. I met him in New York, see, when I used to go up his house, he lived on 141st Street.
That's right, 141st Street.
Yeah.
Up the hill there.
